comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! 👋I’m Tadej from Databox. Today we’re launching Databox CLI, bringing Databox directly into your terminal. For most people, Databox lives in a browser tab. You log in, check dashboards, and manage your analytics in the app. Meanwhile, teams increasingly use scripts, data pipelines, CI jobs, and AI coding agents to move data between systems, configure tools, and automate repetitive tasks.Until now, bringing Databox into those workflows meant working directly with our API, writing and maintaining custom code, handling authentication, retries, and errors, and checking that everything worked as expected.This is exactly the kind of friction we want to remove as part of our broader vision to open up the Databox platform, making it easier for people and AI agents to work with Databox through the tools they already use.That's why we built Databox CLI. It brings the capabilities of our public API directly into your terminal, so you can build dashboards and metrics, manage your data, and automate repetitive tasks in Databox using simple commands. Here’s what you can do with it:Create datasets with defined schemas: set column types and primary keys, and validate records before they’re ingested. Bring in data from anywhere: Load JSON data from files, scripts, or directly from pipelines. For example: curl -s https://api.internal/export | databox dataset ingest DATASET_IDVerify every ingestion: Confirm that your data arrived successfully and see exactly what went wrong if it didn't.Build metrics: Create metrics on top of your datasets and trace where the data comes from.Manage your Databox account: Work with users, permissions, databoards, and connections.That's 91 commands across 14 areas, with a 1:1 match to the Databox public API.And you can let AI coding agents do the work for you, too.Databox CLI comes with 10 ready-to-use agent skills for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and other compatible coding agents. Commands support structured JSON output with --json, clear exit codes, and errors that explain what went wrong. Idempotency keys make retries safe, and destructive actions require an explicit --force flag.Want to try it?Getting started takes three commands:npm install -g databox-clidatabox auth logindatabox account listTo add the agent skills: npx skills add databox/databox-cli --skill '*'Databox CLI is available on all Databox plans and is open source under the MIT license.: github.com/databox/databox-cli, available as a node npm package https://www.npmjs.com/package/databox-cli. today.name: ProtoMap
today.tagline: Stop wasting AI tokens rediscovering dependencies
today.description: ProtoMap helps engineers and AI coding agents understand how services, APIs, and data fields depend on each other across large codebases. It builds a deterministic dependency map for gRPC and Protobuf systems, updated on every commit and accessible through a web app or MCP. Instead of wasting time and tokens searching code across repositories, agents query ProtoMap directly to understand change impact. One enterprise team reduced change-planning time and tokens by 8×.

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt! I'm Amjad, co-founder of HoundDog.ai. Today we're launching ProtoMap.The problemAI coding agents are writing more of our code every day, and every line adds services, calls and fields that the next agent has to rediscover. In a large gRPC + Protobuf codebase, a simple question like "what breaks if I change this service, RPC or field?" sends an agent off to grep, find and read files across repos, trying to piece together relationships in code that often isn't even checked out on the developer's machine. That's slow and expensive, the answer is often incomplete, and it changes from one run to the next.How ProtoMap is different 🚀ProtoMap doesn't replace your coding agent. It gives your agent the context it is missing. A deterministic static-analysis engine maps every service, API and field across your monorepos and microservices, refreshes the map on every commit, and serves it to engineers in a web platform and to coding agents over MCP.🔹 Multi-hop service dependencies: see the blast radius of a change up to five hops out.🔹 Method dependencies: find who calls an RPC, plus every call site with its file location.🔹 Field dependencies: see which services and repos send or receive a field like credit_card.🔹 Code owners: see every inbound service, plus the maintainers and dependents to notify.🔹 Unused RPCs: find dead RPCs, orphaned calls, and proto messages declared differently in two repos.Because agents query the graph instead of re-reading code, the cost of an answer depends on the question, not on the size of your codebase. For one enterprise customer with a monorepo of millions of lines and a complex web of gRPC services, ProtoMap reduced the time and tokens required for change planning by 8×.Who is it for?Engineering teams running gRPC + Protobuf at scale, and the AI coding agents working alongside them.BenchmarkIn the gallery video, you’ll see two live Claude Code sessions (Opus 5.5, high effort) running side by side, given the same prompt at the same moment and recorded on one screen.The prompt:"We want to remove the RPC acme.documents.v1.DocumentQueryService/ResolveDocuments. Find every place in every repo that calls it, including indirect calls through helpers, method names built from strings, registries, or reflection, and give file:line and the calling service for each so we can migrate them."On this prompt, ProtoMap was 7× faster and 36× cheaper, and used 93× fewer tokens:■ Claude Code alone (no MCP): 6:01 · $14.44 · 24.5M tokens■ Claude Code + ProtoMap MCP: 0:50 · $0.40 · 262K tokensFor more detailed benchmarks across 20 prompts on 9 gRPC repositories, see our benchmark page: https://hounddog.ai/protomap-benchmark/Live DemoVisit https://hounddog.ai/videos/protomap-demo/ to see our live demo at MozFest, which includes querying the service graph in our web platform to track dependencies for services, APIs and fields across multiple hops, including callers, callees and call sites. The demo also walks through our detailed benchmarks.🔗 Get startedProtoMap is free to run on your machine: the self-hosted web platform and CLI scanner. When you're ready to roll it out org-wide, the Enterprise plan keeps the graph fresh across every repo, with CI scans on every pull request and GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab integrations. Get started at https://github.com/hounddogai/protomap We'd love your feedback, especially from anyone managing a large gRPC codebase!

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
